sections.h2: Which Montgomery County offices deal with property tax?
sections.html:
Valuation and collection sit in different buildings of the Mt. Sterling courthouse complex. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) decides what each parcel is worth. The Sheriff's Office prints and collects the bills.

  • PVA, (859) 498-8710: questions about value, the tax roll and exemption forms.
  • Sheriff, (859) 498-8704: amounts due. Checks go to 1 Court Street, Suite 4, Mt. Sterling, KY 40353, with the bill number written on them.
  • County Clerk, (859) 498-8700: recording a deed, and any bill that has gone delinquent.

The sheriff's site lets you view and print bills and receipts but offers no way to pay on the web. Anyone who wants a receipt mailed back should enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope with the check.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Montgomery County itself?
sections.html:
Land in the county rises and falls between 707 and 1,447 feet above sea level, across 197 square miles of the Outer Bluegrass. Clark County gave up the territory in 1796. The Census Bureau estimates 28,822 residents for 2025, a gain of 2.5% since the 2020 base.

Mount Sterling, the seat, lies 34 miles east of Lexington. Interstate 64 clips the north edge of town at exits 110 and 113, while U.S. 60 and U.S. 460 cross downtown. Workers here report an average commute of 25.7 minutes. Wikipedia describes the area as a micropolitan area inside the Lexington combined statistical area, and notes that Mount Sterling is a wet city in an otherwise dry county for package alcohol.

Zoning is uneven. The fiscal court says there is no countywide planning and zoning, yet subdivisions within five miles of Mt. Sterling must meet the city's zoning and subdivision rules. Anyone planning to split a lot before a sale should call city hall first. Each October, Court Day brings roughly 130,000 visitors to downtown over four days, which is worth knowing before scheduling showings that weekend.

sections.h2: How does Montgomery County housing look in Census data?
sections.html:
QuickFacts gives a picture of a county with a sizable rental segment and moderate prices. The figures below cover 2020 to 2024 unless noted.

  • 12,422 housing units in 2025, and 53 building permits that year.
  • Homeowners live in 68.3% of occupied units, leaving close to a third to renters.
  • A typical owned home is worth $172,200.
  • Monthly ownership costs are $1,242 for mortgage holders and $470 for owners with no loan.
  • Gross rent has a midpoint of $830.
  • Household income has a midpoint of $56,396, and 15.5% of people live below the poverty line.

Nearly nine in ten residents (88.3%) stayed put during the previous year. A seller with deferred repairs can expect a slower sale than one with a tidy house.

sections.h2: What are the 2026 Montgomery County due dates?
sections.html:
The sheriff reports that 2026 bills were mailed in the last week of September and became payable October 1, 2026. The calendar below is the one the sheriff approved for this tax year.

Sheriff's approved collection dates, 2026 tax year
DatesWhat the bill becomes
10/01/2026 through 11/01/2026Two percent comes off
11/02/2026 through 12/31/2026Printed total, no adjustment
01/01/2027 through 01/31/2027Five percent is tacked on
02/01/2027 through 04/15/2027Twenty-one percent is tacked on

A sheriff's note says a payment made while the 10% penalty applies, before the bill is handed to the clerk, carries one more 10% sheriff's fee. At close of business on April 15, 2027, delinquent bills transfer to the County Clerk. From then on a 20% County Attorney fee, a 10% clerk fee and 1% interest each month apply, and the clerk may sell a bill still unpaid to a third party in summer 2027.

sections.h2: What would a $1,500 Montgomery County bill cost at each stage?
sections.html:
In the discount window it is $1,470. Through December it is $1,500. January raises it to $1,575, and the February to mid-April stretch lifts it to $1,815. Between the best and worst sheriff dates lies $345.

A past-due bill belongs to the clerk after April 15, and the clerk gives the payoff. A seller who owes an earlier year should ask for that figure before picking a closing date. If your lender pays the tax from escrow, or a prior owner is responsible, the sheriff asks that you pass the bill along so it is paid on time.

sections.h2: How can an owner push back on a Montgomery County valuation?
sections.html:
The value reflects the property as of January 1. Under KRS 133.120, the first step is a sit-down with the PVA or a deputy, which can be done by telephone. KRS 133.045 opens the tax roll for inspection for 13 days from the first Monday in May, unless the Department of Revenue picks other dates.

If that talk fails, put your complaint in writing and deliver it to the County Clerk. Name the parcel, say why the number is wrong and state what you believe it is worth. The hearing is before the county appeals board, and the burden is on you to bring evidence such as an appraisal, listings or a builder's estimate.

Pay on your own figure while the case is open. If the final number rises, you owe the difference plus interest. Skipping the county hearing forfeits the later route to the state Board of Tax Appeals.

sections.h2: Does a Montgomery County owner qualify for homestead relief?
sections.html:
Anyone aged 65 or over, or classified as totally disabled, may claim the state exemption, which is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. A home appraised at $172,200 would be taxed as if it were worth $123,100.

Take the form to the PVA. A birth certificate, driver's license or passport proves age. Disability claimants renew yearly, except veterans with a service-connected disability and people ruled permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

sections.h2: How should a Montgomery County seller treat the tax bill at closing?
sections.html:
Whoever owns the house on January 1 is the taxpayer for that year, and a purchase later in the year leaves the bill under the previous owner's name. KRS 134.015 calls the tax a personal debt of that owner. A lien from unpaid tax can last 11 years under KRS 134.420 and passes to the next buyer along with the land.

  • Call the sheriff to learn whether this year's bill is paid and what a payoff would be on the closing date.
  • Decide in the sales contract who bears which months of tax.
  • List the buyer's tax-bill mailing address in the deed, which KRS 382.135 demands.
  • Take the signed deed to the County Clerk for recording.

A title company will search for old bills, so settling any in advance avoids a delay.

faqs.q: Who sends the Montgomery County tax bill?
faqs.a: The Sheriff's Office, which can be reached at (859) 498-8704. Call the PVA at (859) 498-8710 only when the assessed value looks wrong.

faqs.q: Is online payment offered by the Montgomery County Sheriff?
faqs.a: No. Bills and receipts can be viewed and printed on the sheriff's site, but payment goes by mail or in person at 1 Court Street, Suite 4, Mt. Sterling.

faqs.q: What are the penalty periods after December 31 in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: Five percent applies in January and twenty-one percent from February 1 to April 15. Delinquent bills then move to the County Clerk, who adds attorney and clerk fees plus monthly interest.

faqs.q: Is there zoning in Montgomery County outside Mt. Sterling?
faqs.a: There is none countywide. Subdivisions within five miles of Mt. Sterling follow the city's rules, so ask city hall before dividing land.

faqs.q: What does the state homestead exemption take off a Montgomery County home?
faqs.a: It removes $49,100 from the assessed value for 2025 and 2026. The owner must be 65 or older or totally disabled and must apply at the PVA.
